prompt_free_text:
This paper tackles an important and practically motivated problem: open-world product attribute mining under limited supervision. The setting is appealing because it moves beyond both closed-world tagging and zero-shot extraction with predefined target attributes, aiming instead to expand known attribute vocabularies while also discovering previously unseen attribute types automatically. That is a meaningful step toward realistic e-commerce information extraction. The paper also contributes a new dataset, WoaM, and proposes Amacer, a pipeline combining syntax-based candidate generation, supervised contrastive learning from seed attributes, adaptive expansion for known attributes, DBSCAN for residual clustering, and two forms of weak regularization for unseen attributes. Overall, I found the problem formulation timely and the empirical gains substantial, but I also have several concerns about evaluation design, methodological clarity, and the strength of some claims.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the task formulation itself. The distinction from prior work is clear enough: unlike closed-world extraction, the method must handle unseen types; unlike zero-shot extraction, it does not assume the new type names are given at inference time; and unlike prior weakly supervised open-world work, it explicitly targets richer product text including bullet points. This is a realistic and challenging setting. The dataset design also appears thoughtful in several respects. In particular, using a curated seed set rather than noisy distant supervision is a sensible compromise between scalability and quality, and the inclusion of bullet points is valuable because they contain richer and less templatic attribute expressions than titles. The paper does a good job motivating why this setting matters and why existing benchmarks are insufficient.

Methodologically, the paper is also reasonably coherent. The overall pipeline is intuitive: generate broad candidate spans, learn an embedding space where attribute-compatible spans are close, then cluster. The syntax-oriented candidate generation is simple but practical, and the adaptive expansion step for known seed attributes is a nice idea that acknowledges the asymmetry between expanding known types and discovering unknown ones. The use of supervised contrastive learning instead of more cumbersome triplet/regression objectives is sensible. The two additional regularizers for unseen attributes are also interesting: the bullet-point co-occurrence heuristic is lightweight and plausible, and the latent-attribute module is a creative attempt to inject unsupervised structure into the embedding space.

Empirically, the reported improvements are strong. The main result table shows consistent gains over OA-Mine and other baselines, especially under the syntax-based candidate setting. The ablations suggest that each component contributes, and the decomposition by seed/new types and title/bullet points is useful. I particularly appreciated that the paper does not only report aggregate scores but also analyzes the harder subsets, where the regularization seems most beneficial. The qualitative examples are also informative, especially because they reveal both successes and failure modes.

That said, I have several substantive concerns.

My biggest concern is the evaluation protocol and the definition of the main metric. The paper evaluates a task that jointly involves span extraction and clustering, but the reported “pseudo-F1” is derived from averaging Jaccard, ARI, and NMI as a proxy for precision and combining that with recall. This is unconventional and somewhat hard to interpret. Jaccard, ARI, and NMI are clustering agreement metrics with different behaviors and scales; averaging them and treating the result as “precision” is not theoretically justified. Because the paper’s main claims hinge on improvements in this pseudo-F1, the validity of the metric matters a lot. The paper does provide the underlying clustering metrics and recall separately, which helps, but the headline metric remains ad hoc. I would strongly encourage the authors to either adopt a more standard clustering evaluation for open IE-style tasks or provide a much stronger justification that this pseudo-F1 correlates with meaningful end-task quality. At minimum, the paper should emphasize the raw metrics more prominently and avoid overinterpreting the derived F1.

Relatedly, the evaluation seems to conflate several subproblems: candidate generation quality, span boundary quality, attribute assignment for known types, and clustering/discovery for unknown types. The paper partially addresses this by reporting span-only extraction scores and by evaluating with gold spans as candidates in one analysis table, but these analyses are not central enough. Since the proposed method is a pipeline, gains could come disproportionately from candidate generation rather than representation learning or clustering. The paper argues that representation learning matters, and Table 4 helps, but I would have liked a more systematic disentanglement. For example, reporting clustering quality conditioned on correctly extracted spans, or reporting candidate recall/precision before clustering, would make the contributions much clearer.

A second major concern is the limited breadth of the dataset and the resulting uncertainty about generalization. WoaM contains only four product categories, all from Amazon, all in English, and all with a specific title-plus-bullet format. This is a reasonable starting point, but the paper sometimes makes broader claims about practical open-world attribute mining. It is not yet clear whether the approach would transfer to categories with very different linguistic patterns, to noisier marketplaces, or to multilingual settings. The syntax-based candidate generation in particular may be sensitive to domain and language. The authors acknowledge dependence on POS tagging, but the broader issue is that the whole pipeline may be tuned to the structure of Amazon product descriptions. I do not think this invalidates the contribution, but the claims should be calibrated more carefully.

A third concern is that some methodological choices are underjustified or potentially brittle. The candidate generation step relies on POS patterns extracted from product profiles, but the paper does not quantify how many gold spans are excluded by this design, nor how sensitive performance is to the pattern inventory. Since this step is foundational, more analysis is needed. Similarly, the adaptive expansion threshold is based on average intra-seed cosine distance scaled by a global relaxation parameter. This is elegant, but it assumes seed sets are internally coherent and that average pairwise similarity is a good proxy for cluster radius. In heterogeneous attributes, this may fail. The paper should provide more intuition or empirical evidence that this thresholding is robust across categories and attribute types.

The latent-attribute module is interesting but also the least convincing part of the method as currently presented. Conceptually, it resembles neural topic modeling over candidate spans, but the connection between the learned latent attributes and actual product attributes is loose. The qualitative examples show some coherent concepts, but also repetition and collapse. The paper itself notes topic collapse and does not address it. More importantly, it is not entirely clear how much of the gain comes from this module versus the simpler self-supervised bullet-point regularizer. The paper states that the latent attribute formulation contributes around 70% of the regularization improvement, but I did not see a sufficiently detailed ablation in the main text to verify this. Given the added complexity, the paper would benefit from a cleaner isolation of the latent module’s effect, sensitivity to the number of latent attributes K, and perhaps a comparison to simpler unsupervised regularizers such as product-level contrastive objectives or clustering consistency losses.

I also have concerns about baseline fairness and completeness. The paper compares against OA-Mine and tagging-based baselines, which is appropriate, but the open-world clustering baselines are somewhat narrow. Since the method’s core is embedding learning plus clustering, stronger metric-learning or sentence-embedding baselines would be useful. For example, one could compare against SBERT-style contrastive fine-tuning with standard clustering, or against recent unsupervised/open IE clustering methods adapted to this setting. The paper uses the same BERT-Large encoder for all models, which is good for fairness, but some baselines appear disadvantaged by design choices inherited from their original settings. In particular, closed-world tagging models are almost guaranteed to underperform on unseen types, so their inclusion is useful mainly as a lower bound, not as a serious competitor. The more relevant comparison is against strong weakly supervised open-world alternatives under the same candidate set and encoder.

Another issue is annotation and reproducibility detail. The test set is annotated by two in-house annotators, but the paper does not report inter-annotator agreement, adjudication procedure, or detailed annotation guidelines beyond non-overlap and single-label assignment. In an open-world attribute setting, boundary decisions and type granularity are inherently subjective, so agreement statistics are important. The seed set construction also involves human curation and type splitting/merging, but the exact criteria are not fully specified. Since the dataset is a major contribution, stronger documentation of annotation quality would significantly improve confidence in the benchmark.

There are also some conceptual ambiguities around what counts as a “reasonable attribute.” The paper says annotators label spans that appear as reasonable attribute values of either existing or brand-new types that fit the context. This leaves room for substantial subjectivity. For example, some extracted spans in the qualitative examples look more like topical phrases, claims, or usage contexts than canonical product attributes. That may be acceptable if the benchmark intentionally embraces a broad notion of attributes, but then the paper should define this notion more precisely and discuss its implications. Otherwise, models may be rewarded for clustering semantically related phrases that are not truly attributes in a structured catalog sense.

On the technical presentation side, the paper is generally understandable, but there are several places where clarity could be improved. The loss notation is occasionally inconsistent, and some equations appear to have formatting issues. The supervised contrastive loss denominator seems to exclude positives entirely rather than using the standard all-other-samples denominator; if intentional, this should be explained. The description of the unsupervised ELBO is also somewhat compressed, and it is not fully clear how candidate spans are batched, how duplicate spans are handled, or how the latent attribute embeddings interact with the encoder during optimization. There are also many grammatical issues throughout the paper. They do not prevent understanding, but they do reduce polish and occasionally create ambiguity.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper has real merit. The problem is important, the dataset is potentially valuable, and the empirical results are promising. The work is especially compelling as a practical systems paper: it shows that a relatively simple but carefully designed pipeline, augmented with weak semantic regularization, can outperform prior weakly supervised open-world methods on a harder benchmark. I also appreciate that the authors are candid about limitations, including noisy candidate spans and topic collapse.

For improvement, I would most strongly recommend the following. First, strengthen the evaluation section: either replace the pseudo-F1 with a more standard metric or justify it much more carefully, and provide clearer decomposition of candidate generation versus clustering quality. Second, add more annotation-quality details for the dataset, including agreement and adjudication. Third, expand the ablation study for the regularization components, especially isolating self-supervised versus latent-attribute effects and sensitivity to K. Fourth, provide more analysis of candidate generation coverage and failure modes, since this step is central to the method’s success. Fifth, calibrate claims about generality and practicality given the limited category and language scope.

My overall assessment is positive but not unequivocal. I see this as a meaningful contribution with strong practical motivation and solid empirical gains, but one whose evaluation methodology and dataset documentation need to be stronger for a top-tier venue. If accepted, the paper would likely stimulate useful follow-up work on open-world attribute extraction under weak supervision. If rejected, it would still be close to the bar and could become significantly stronger with improved evaluation rigor and clearer analysis.

Recommendation: weak accept to borderline accept, depending on venue standards for evaluation rigor. The novelty of the task setting and dataset, together with the practical effectiveness of the approach, are compelling; the main weaknesses are the unconventional evaluation metric, limited dataset scope, and insufficiently rigorous analysis of annotation quality and component contributions.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper introduces a new lightly supervised open-world product attribute mining setting, where a model must both expand known seed attribute types and discover previously unseen attribute types from e-commerce text. To support this setting, the authors construct the WoaM dataset across four Amazon product categories with curated seed attributes and human-annotated test data. They propose Amacer, a pipeline consisting of syntax-based candidate span generation using POS patterns, supervised contrastive representation learning from seed attributes, adaptive expansion for assigning candidates to seed types, DBSCAN for additional clustering, and two regularizers for unseen attributes: a self-supervised bullet-point co-occurrence objective and an unsupervised latent-attribute topic-model-like objective. Experiments show improvements over OA-Mine and tagging baselines on their dataset, especially in partial-match F1 and on new attribute types.
strengths: Addresses a practically relevant and underexplored setting: open-world attribute mining with limited supervision rather than fully supervised closed-world extraction.
Introduces a new dataset with explicit emphasis on unseen attribute types and richer product context beyond titles, which is valuable for future work.
The overall system design is intuitive and modular: candidate generation, representation learning, seed expansion, and new-cluster discovery are clearly separated.
The syntax-based candidate generation is simple, efficient, and empirically stronger than segmentation-based alternatives on this benchmark.
The use of additional implicit signals for unseen attributes is a reasonable idea, and the ablations suggest the regularization contributes measurable gains.
The paper includes useful decomposed analyses for seed vs. new attributes and title vs. bullet-point text, helping clarify where gains arise.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is nonstandard and somewhat ad hoc: the main metric defines 'pseudo precision' as the average of Jaccard, ARI, and NMI, then derives a pseudo-F1 with recall. This combination lacks clear theoretical justification and makes it hard to interpret practical significance.

The proposed supervised contrastive loss appears incorrectly specified: the denominator excludes positives and possibly the anchor itself, differing from standard supervised contrastive formulations. This raises concerns about whether the implemented objective matches the paper.

The latent-attribute model is only loosely connected to attribute discovery and appears underdeveloped; the paper itself notes topic collapse and repetitive latent attributes, suggesting the mechanism may be unstable.
The method is heavily pipeline-dependent, and candidate span quality remains a major bottleneck; span extraction exact F1 is below 37 even for the best model, limiting end-to-end usefulness.
The dataset is limited to only four product categories, so claims about general open-world product attribute mining may be overstated.

Comparison fairness is imperfect because several baselines are adapted to a new dataset/setting, while the proposed method benefits from a custom candidate generator and grouping strategy tailored to the benchmark.
methodological_flaws: The supervised contrastive objective in Section 4 is mathematically questionable. In standard supervised contrastive learning, the denominator includes all non-anchor examples (including positives), whereas here it is defined only over negatives. This changes the optimization behavior substantially and may make the stated connection to supervised contrastive learning inaccurate.

The self-supervised contrastive loss in Section 6 repeats the same denominator issue, again deviating from standard InfoNCE/supervised contrastive formulations. If this is not a typo, the scientific justification for the loss is weak; if it is a typo, the paper is mathematically imprecise in a central component.

The variational latent-attribute formulation is not rigorously specified. Equation (3) uses a linear map for both mean and variance without ensuring positivity of the variance parameter; in practice one would need log-variance or softplus. As written, the Gaussian parameterization is invalid.

The ELBO description is imprecise/inconsistent: the KL term is written as KL(\tilde{\alpha}^p || \hat{\alpha}), but \tilde{\alpha}^p is sampled pre-softmax logits while \hat{\alpha} is described as a standard Gaussian prior Product-to-Attribute distribution. The notation conflates Gaussian latent variables and simplex probabilities, obscuring what distribution the KL is actually computed over.

The adaptive expansion threshold uses the average pairwise cosine distance among seeds as a threshold. Since cosine distance depends strongly on seed-set diversity, this heuristic can perversely make semantically broad attributes easier to absorb noisy candidates and narrow attributes harder to expand. No formal or empirical calibration analysis is provided.

The main empirical claim of statistical significance is under-specified: only a t-test with '>95% confidence' is mentioned, without stating the number of runs, what constitutes an independent sample, or whether assumptions of the test hold.

The evaluation metric mixes clustering quality metrics computed only on matched/gold spans with a separate recall term over extraction coverage, then compresses them into pseudo-F1. This can distort model ranking and does not correspond to a standard objective for joint extraction and clustering.

Because the seed set is bootstrapped from retailer-provided product profiles and then string-matched into the corpus, there is potential leakage of lexical patterns and attribute values closely aligned with the test distribution. The paper does not sufficiently analyze how much performance comes from this resource construction choice versus true open-world generalization.
